**Proposed mechanism:** STK11 pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ STK11 (HGNC:11174); STK11 (HGNC:11174) —DISRUPTS→ intestinal polyp formation (null); intestinal polyp formation (null) —LEADS_TO→ Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (MONDO:0008280); PRKAG2 pathogenic variant (null) —DISRUPTS→ PRKAG2 (HGNC:9343); PRKAG2 (HGNC:9343) —DISRUPTS→ cardiac myocyte function and sarcomere organization (null); cardiac myocyte function and sarcomere organization (null) —LEADS_TO→ Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (MONDO:0008685). Loss-of-function mutations in STK11 lead to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome by disrupting intestinal polyp formation. Gain-of-function or specific missense variants in PRKAG2 lead to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome by disrupting cardiac myocyte function and sarcomere organization. The convergence occurs at the level of cellular function and structural integrity within cardiomyocytes, which can be affected by dysregulation of AMPK subunits (PRKAG2) and potentially indirectly by systemic effects related to PJS, though the primary link is PRKAG2's role in cardiac physiology.

**How to falsify it:** Absence of PRKAG2 variants in individuals with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome who do not exhibit other known causes, or demonstration that STK11 mutations have no discernible effect on cardiac function in any patient cohort. _(variant: null)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared pathways and potential for PRKAG2 involvement in both conditions could lead to improved risk stratification and therapeutic strategies for cardiac complications in patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and potentially identify novel therapeutic targets for WPW by exploring the broader regulatory roles of STK11 and its interactions.
